Suppose you want to print a GIF image located in a file. First, find out whether there is a print service that is capable of handling the task. The static lookupPrintServices method of the PrintServiceLookup class returns an array of PrintService objects that can handle the given document flavor.

DocFlavor flavor = DocFlavor.INPUT_STREAM.GIF;
PrintService[] services = PrintServiceLookup.lookupPrintServices(flavor, null);

The second argument of the lookupPrintServices method is null to indicate that we don’t want to constrain the search by specifying printer attributes. We'll cover attributes in the next section.

If the lookup yields an array with more than one element, select from the listed print services. You can call the getName method of the PrintService class to get the printer names and let the user choose.

Next, get a document print job from the service: 

DocPrintJob job = services[i].createPrintJob();

For printing, you need an object that implements the Doc interface. The Java library supplies a class SimpleDoc for that purpose. The SimpleDoc constructor requires the data source object, the document flavor, and an optional attribute set. For example,

var in = new FileInputStream(fileName);
var doc = new SimpleDoc(in, flavor, null);

Finally, you are ready to print:

job.print(doc, null);

As before, the null argument can be replaced by an attribute set.

Note that this printing process is quite different from that of the preceding section. There is no user interaction through print dialog boxes. For example, you can implement a server-side printing mechanism in which users submit print jobs through a web form.

javax.print.PrintServiceLookup1.4

  • PrintService[] lookupPrintServices(DocFlavor flavor, AttributeSet attributes)

    looks up the print services that can handle the given document flavor and attributes. The attributes parameter can be null if there are no attributes to consider.

javax.print.PrintService1.4

  • DocPrintJob createPrintJob()

    creates a print job for printing an object of a class that implements the Doc interface, such as a SimpleDoc.

javax.print.DocPrintJob1.4

  • void print(Doc doc, PrintRequestAttributeSet attributes)

    prints the given document with the given attributes. The attributes parameter can be null if no printing attributes are required.

javax.print.SimpleDoc1.4

  • SimpleDoc(Object data, DocFlavor flavor, DocAttributeSet attributes)

    constructs a SimpleDoc object that can be printed with a DocPrintJob. The data parameter is the object with the print data, such as an input stream or a Printable. The attributes parameter can be null if attributes are not required.

12.7.4. Stream Print Services

A print service sends print data to a printer. A stream print service generates the same print data but instead sends them to a stream, perhaps for delayed printing or because the print data format can be interpreted by other programs. In particular, if the print data format is PostScript, it may be useful to save the print data to a file because many programs can process PostScript files. The Java platform includes a stream print service that can produce PostScript output from images and 2D graphics. You can use that service on all systems, even if there are no local printers.

Enumerating stream print services is a bit more tedious than locating regular print services. You need both the DocFlavor of the object to be printed and the MIME type of the stream output. You then get a StreamPrintServiceFactory array of factories.

DocFlavor flavor = DocFlavor.SERVICE_FORMATTED.PRINTABLE;
String mimeType = "application/postscript";
StreamPrintServiceFactory[] factories
    = StreamPrintServiceFactory.lookupStreamPrintServiceFactories(flavor, mimeType);

The StreamPrintServiceFactory class has no methods that would help us distinguish any one factory from another, so we just take factories[0]. We call the getPrintService method with an output stream parameter to get a StreamPrintService object.

var out = new FileOutputStream(fileName);
StreamPrintService service = factories[0].getPrintService(out);

The StreamPrintService class is a subclass of PrintService. To produce a printout, simply follow the steps of the preceding section.

javax.print.StreamPrintServiceFactory1.4

  • StreamPrintServiceFactory[] lookupStreamPrintServiceFactories(DocFlavor flavor, String mimeType)

    looks up the stream print service factories that can print the given document flavor and produce an output stream of the given MIME type.

  • StreamPrintService getPrintService(OutputStream out)

    gets a print service that sends the printing output to the given output stream.

The program in Listing 12.29 demonstrates how to use a stream print service to print Java 2D shapes to a PostScript file. You can replace the sample drawing code with code that generates any Java 2D shapes and have the shapes converted to PostScript. Then you can easily convert the result to PDF or EPS, using an external tool. (Unfortunately, Java does not support printing to PDF directly.)

In this example, we call a draw method that draws Java 2D shapes onto a Graphics2D object. If you want to draw the surface of a component (for example, a table or tree), use the following code:

private static int IMAGE_WIDTH = component.getWidth();
private static int IMAGE_HEIGHT = component.getHeight();
public static void draw(Graphics2D g2) { component.paint(g2); }
Listing 12.29 v2ch12/printService/PrintServiceDemo.java 
package v2ch12.printService;

import module java.base;
import module java.desktop;

/**
 * This program demonstrates the use of stream print services. The program prints Java 2D
 * shapes to a PostScript file. If you don't supply a file name on the command line, the output
 * is saved to out.ps.
 */
class PrintServiceDemo {
    // Set your image dimensions here
    int IMAGE_WIDTH = 300;
    int IMAGE_HEIGHT = 300;

    void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String fileName = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "out.ps";
        DocFlavor flavor = DocFlavor.SERVICE_FORMATTED.PRINTABLE;
        String mimeType = "application/postscript";
        StreamPrintServiceFactory[] factories = StreamPrintServiceFactory
                .lookupStreamPrintServiceFactories(flavor, mimeType);
        var out = new FileOutputStream(fileName);
        if (factories.length > 0) {
            PrintService service = factories[0].getPrintService(out);
            var doc = new SimpleDoc(new Printable() {
                public int print(Graphics g, PageFormat pf, int page) {
                    if (page >= 1)
                        return Printable.NO_SUCH_PAGE;
                    else {
                        double sf1 = pf.getImageableWidth() / (IMAGE_WIDTH + 1);
                        double sf2 = pf.getImageableHeight() / (IMAGE_HEIGHT + 1);
                        double s = Math.min(sf1, sf2);
                        var g2 = (Graphics2D) g;
                        g2.translate((pf.getWidth() - pf.getImageableWidth()) / 2,
                                (pf.getHeight() - pf.getImageableHeight()) / 2);
                        g2.scale(s, s);

                        draw(g2);
                        return Printable.PAGE_EXISTS;
                    }
                }
            }, flavor, null);
            DocPrintJob job = service.createPrintJob();
            var attributes = new HashPrintRequestAttributeSet();
            job.print(doc, attributes);
        }
        else
            IO.println("No factories for " + mimeType);
    }
    void draw(Graphics2D g2) {
        // Your drawing instructions go here
        FontRenderContext context = g2.getFontRenderContext();
        var f = new Font("Serif", Font.PLAIN, 72);
        var clipShape = new GeneralPath();

        var layout = new TextLayout("Hello", f, context);
        AffineTransform transform = AffineTransform.getTranslateInstance(0, 72);
        Shape outline = layout.getOutline(transform);
        clipShape.append(outline, false);

        layout = new TextLayout("World", f, context);
        transform = AffineTransform.getTranslateInstance(0, 144);
        outline = layout.getOutline(transform);
        clipShape.append(outline, false);

        g2.draw(clipShape);
        g2.clip(clipShape);

        final int NLINES = 50;
        var p = new Point2D.Double(0, 0);
        for (int i = 0; i < NLINES; i++) {
            double x = (2 * IMAGE_WIDTH * i) / NLINES;
            double y = (2 * IMAGE_HEIGHT * (NLINES - 1 - i)) / NLINES;
            var q = new Point2D.Double(x, y);
            g2.draw(new Line2D.Double(p, q));
        }
    }
}

12.7.5. Printing Attributes

The print service API contains a complex set of interfaces and classes to specify various kinds of attributes. There are four important groups of attributes. The first two specify requests to the printer.

  • Print request attributes request particular features for all doc objects in a print job, such as two-sided printing or the paper size.

  • Doc attributes are request attributes that apply only to a single doc object.

The other two attributes contain information about the printer and job status.

  • Print service attributes give information about the print service, such as the printer make and model or whether the printer is currently accepting jobs.

  • Print job attributes give information about the status of a particular print job, such as whether the job is already completed.

To describe the various attributes, there is an interface Attribute with subinterfaces:

PrintRequestAttribute
DocAttribute
PrintServiceAttribute
PrintJobAttribute
SupportedValuesAttribute

Individual attribute classes implement one or more of these interfaces. For example, objects of the Copies class describe the number of copies of a printout. That class implements both the PrintRequestAttribute and the PrintJobAttribute interfaces. Clearly, a print request can contain a request for multiple copies. Conversely, an attribute of the print job might be how many of these copies were actually printed. That number might be lower, perhaps because of printer limitations or because the printer ran out of paper.

The SupportedValuesAttribute interface indicates that an attribute value does not reflect actual request or status data but rather the capability of a service. For example, the CopiesSupported class implements the SupportedValuesAttribute interface. An object of that class might describe that a printer supports 1 through 99 copies of a printout.

Figure 12.65 shows a class diagram of the attribute hierarchy.

Figure 12.65: The attribute hierarchy

In addition to the interfaces and classes for individual attributes, the print service API defines interfaces and classes for attribute sets. A superinterface, AttributeSet, has four subinterfaces: 

PrintRequestAttributeSet
DocAttributeSet
PrintServiceAttributeSet
PrintJobAttributeSet

Each of these interfaces has an implementing class, yielding the five classes: 

HashAttributeSet
HashPrintRequestAttributeSet
HashDocAttributeSet
HashPrintServiceAttributeSet
HashPrintJobAttributeSet

Figure 12.66 shows a class diagram of the attribute set hierarchy.

Figure 12.66: The attribute set hierarchy

For example, you can construct a print request attribute set like this:

var attributes = new HashPrintRequestAttributeSet();

After constructing the set, you are freed from worrying about the Hash prefix.

Why have all these interfaces? They make it possible to check for correct attribute usage. For example, a DocAttributeSet accepts only objects that implement the DocAttribute interface. Any attempt to add another attribute results in a runtime error.

An attribute set is a specialized kind of map where the keys are of type Class and the values belong to a class that implements the Attribute interface. For example, if you insert an object

new Copies(10)

into an attribute set, then its key is the Class object Copies.class. That key is called the category of the attribute. The Attribute interface declares a method 

Class getCategory()

that returns the category of an attribute. The Copies class defines the method to return the object Copies.class, but it isn’t a requirement that the category be the same as the class of the attribute.

When an attribute is added to an attribute set, the category is extracted automatically. Just add the attribute value: 

attributes.add(new Copies(10));

If you subsequently add another attribute with the same category, it overwrites the first one.

To retrieve an attribute, you need to use the category as the key, for example: 

AttributeSet attributes = job.getAttributes();
var copies = (Copies) attributes.get(Copies.class);

Finally, attributes are organized by the values they can have. The Copies attribute can have any integer value. The Copies class extends the IntegerSyntax class that takes care of all integer-valued attributes. The getValue method returns the integer value of the attribute, for example: 

int n = copies.getValue();

The classes

TextSyntax
DateTimeSyntax
URISyntax

encapsulate a string, a date and time value, or a URI.

Finally, many attributes can take a finite number of values. For example, the PrintQuality attribute has three settings: draft, normal, and high. They are represented by three constants:

PrintQuality.DRAFT
PrintQuality.NORMAL
PrintQuality.HIGH

Attribute classes with a finite number of values extend the EnumSyntax class, which provides a number of convenience methods to set up these enumerations in a typesafe manner. You need not worry about the mechanism when using such an attribute. Simply add the named values to attribute sets:

attributes.add(PrintQuality.HIGH);

Here is how you check the value of an attribute: 

if (attributes.get(PrintQuality.class) == PrintQuality.HIGH)
    . . .

Table 12.5 lists the printing attributes. The second column lists the superclass of the attribute class (for example, IntegerSyntax for the Copies attribute) or the set of enumeration values for the attributes with a finite set of values. The last four columns indicate whether the attribute class implements the DocAttribute (D), PrintJobAttribute (J), PrintRequestAttribute (R), and PrintServiceAttribute (S) interfaces.

You have now reached the end of this long chapter covering advanced Swing and AWT features. In the final chapter, we will turn to a different aspect of Java programming: interacting, on the same machine, with “native” code in a different programming language.

Chapter 13 ▪ The Foreign Functions and Memory API

While a “100% Pure Java” solution is nice in principle, there are situations in which you will want to write (or use) code in another language. Such code is usually called native code.

Particularly in the early days of Java, many people assumed that it would be a good idea to use C or C++ to speed up critical parts of a Java application. However, in practice, this was rarely useful. A presentation at the 1996 JavaOne conference showed this clearly. The developers of the cryptography library at Sun Microsystems reported that a pure Java platform implementation of their cryptographic functions was more than adequate. It was true that the code was not as fast as a C implementation would have been, but it turned out not to matter. The Java platform implementation was far faster than the network I/O. This turned out to be the real bottleneck.

Since then, the just-in-time compiler has become far better, and it is not common to turn to native code just for performance. But there are other valid reasons, such as these:

  • Your application requires access to system features or devices that are not accessible through the Java platform.

  • You have substantial amounts of tested and debugged code in another language.

For example, consider using an artificial intelligence library that was written in C or C++, and that uses GPUs. It may not be practical to reimplement it in Java. In such a case, a bridge between Java and native code becomes necessary.

Ever since Java 1.1, the Java platform had an API for interoperating with native C code called the Java Native Interface (JNI).

However, as you will see, there is a certain amount of tedium involved in using JNI. Java 17 introduced, as a preview feature, an API to access “foreign” functions and memory that is quite a bit more convenient than JNI. This FFM API has now become a regular feature of Java 25.

We'll start the chapter by giving you a brief flavor of JNI, and then turn to the FFM API. You should use that API for new projects. At some point in the future, JNI is likely to become deprecated.

Of course, there are drawbacks to going native. If a part of your application is written in another language, you must supply a separate native library for every platform you want to support. Code written in C or C++ offers no protection against overwriting memory through invalid pointer usage. It is easy to write native methods that corrupt your program or infect the operating system.

For that reason, since Java 22, you must opt in to native access (whether through JNI or the FFM API). If you do not use modules, start the program as

java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED ...

In a modular program, list the modules for which native access is allowed:

java --enable-native-access=module1, module2 ...

13.1. Using JNI to Call C Code from a Java Program

Suppose you have a C function that does something you like and, for one reason or another, you don’t want to bother reimplementing it in Java. For the sake of illustration, we'll call the C printf function with one argument.

With JNI, you need to declare a proxy method using the keyword native, and you will obviously need to place the method in a class. The result is shown in Listing 13.1.

The native keyword alerts the compiler that the method will be defined externally. Of course, native methods will contain no Java code, and the method header is followed immediately by a terminating semicolon. Therefore, native method declarations look similar to abstract method declarations.

Listing 13.1 v2ch13/jnidemo/HelloNative.java 
package v2ch13.jnidemo;

class HelloNative {  
    public static native int printf(String str);
}

In this particular example, the native method is also declared as static. Native methods can be both static and nonstatic.

You can actually compile this class, but if you try to use it in a program, the virtual machine will tell you it doesn’t know how to find printf—reporting an UnsatisfiedLinkError. To implement the native code, write a corresponding C function. You must name that function exactly the way the Java virtual machine expects. Here are the rules:

  1. Use the full Java method name, such as jnidemo.HelloNative.printf.

  2. Replace every period with an underscore, and append the prefix Java_. For example, Java_jnidemo_HelloNative_printf.

  3. If the class name contains characters that are not ASCII letters or digits—that is, '_', '$', or Unicode characters with codes greater than \u007F—replace them with _0xxxx, where xxxx is the sequence of four hexadecimal digits of the character's Unicode value.

If you overload native methods—that is, if you provide multiple native methods with the same name—you must append a double underscore followed by the encoded argument types. For example, if you have a native method greeting() and another native method greeting(int repeat), then the first one is called Java_jnidemo_HelloNative_greeting__ and the second, Java_jnidemo_HelloNative_greeting__I.

Actually, nobody does this by hand; instead, run javac with the -h flag, providing the directory in which the header files should be placed:

javac -h v2ch13/jnidemo v2ch13/jnidemo/HelloNative.java

This command creates a header file v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative.h, as shown in Listing 13.2.

Listing 13.2 v2ch13/jnidemo/v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative.h 
/* DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE - it is machine generated */
#include <jni.h>
/* Header for class v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative */

#ifndef _Included_v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative
#define _Included_v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative
#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif
/*
 * Class:     v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative
 * Method:    printf
 * Signature: (Ljava/lang/String;)I
 */
JNIEXPORT jint JNICALL Java_v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative_printf
  (JNIEnv *, jclass, jstring);

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif
#endif

As you can see, this file contains the declaration of a function Java_v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative_printf. (The macros JNIEXPORT and JNICALL are defined in the header file jni.h. They denote compiler-dependent specifiers for exported functions that come from a dynamically loaded library.)

Now, copy the function prototype from the header file into a source file and give the implementation code for the function, as shown in Listing 13.3.

You can use C++ to implement native methods. However, you must then declare the functions that implement the native methods as extern "C". (This stops the C++ compiler from “mangling” the method name.) For example, 

extern "C"
JNIEXPORT int JNICALL Java_v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative_printf(JNIEnv* env,
    jclass cl, . . .) { . . . }
Listing 13.3 v2ch13/jnidemo/HelloNative.c 
#include "v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative.h"
#include <stdio.h>

JNIEXPORT jint JNICALL Java_v2ch13_jnidemo_HelloNative_printf(
        JNIEnv *env, jclass cl, jstring jstr) {
    const char *cstr = (*env)->GetStringUTFChars(env, jstr, NULL);
    int numchars = printf(cstr);
    (*env)->ReleaseStringUTFChars(env, jstr, cstr);
    return numchars;
}

We will not delve deeply into this code, but there are a couple of highlights.

Each native function receives a parameter env that is needed to access the C API for native calls. You can see an example in the call to (*env)->GetStringUTFChars(...).

The cl parameter is a descriptor of the Java class. In an instance method, you would instead get a descriptor to the object on which the native method was invoked.

Next, let's look at how to transfer strings to native methods. A native method with a String parameter receives a value of an opaque type called jstring. Strings are quite different in the two languages: In Java, they are sequences of UTF-16 code points, whereas C strings are null-terminated sequences of bytes. JNI has two sets of functions for manipulating strings: One converts Java strings to “modified UTF-8” byte sequences and another converts them to arrays of UTF-16 values. (The UTF-8, “modified UTF-8,” and UTF-16 formats were discussed in Chapter 2. Recall that the UTF-8 and “modified UTF-8” encodings leave ASCII characters unchanged, but all other Unicode characters are encoded as multibyte sequences.)

The standard UTF-8 encoding and the “modified UTF-8” encoding differ for characters with codes higher than 0xFFFF. In the standard UTF-8 encoding, these characters are encoded as 4-byte sequences. In the “modified” encoding, each such character is first encoded as a pair of “surrogates” in the UTF-16 encoding, and then each surrogate is encoded with UTF-8, yielding a total of 6 bytes. This is clumsy, but it is a historical accident—the JVM specification was written when Unicode was still limited to 16 bits.

In our example, we call printf and therefore convert to UTF-8. Had we used the “wide” version wprintf, UTF-16 would have been appropriate.

To read the contents of an existing jstring object, use the GetStringUTFChars function. This function returns a pointer to the “modified UTF-8” characters that describe the character string. Note that a specific virtual machine is free to choose this character encoding for its internal string representation, so you might get a character pointer into the actual Java string. Since Java strings are meant to be immutable, it is very important that you treat the const seriously and do not try to write into this character array. On the other hand, if the virtual machine uses UTF-16 or UTF-32 characters for its internal string representation, this function call allocates a new memory block that will be filled with the “modified UTF-8” equivalents.

The virtual machine must know when you are finished using the string so that it can garbage-collect it. (The garbage collector runs in a separate thread, and it can interrupt the execution of native methods.) For that reason, you must call the ReleaseStringUTFChars function.

Compile the native C code into a dynamically loaded library. The details depend on your compiler.

For example, with the GNU C compiler on Linux, use these commands:

gcc -fPIC -I $JAVA_HOME/include -I $JAVA_HOME/include/linux -shared \
    -o v2ch13/jnidemo/libHelloNative.so v2ch13/jnidemo/HelloNative.c

With the Microsoft compiler under Windows, the command is

cd v2ch13/jnidemo
cl -I %JAVA_HOME%\include -I %JAVA_HOME%\include\win32 ^
    -LD HelloNative.c -FeHelloNative.dll

Finally, add a call to the System.loadLibrary method in your program. To ensure that the virtual machine will load the library before the first use of the class, use a static initialization block, as in Listing 13.4.

Figure 13.1: Processing native code
Listing 13.4 v2ch13/jnidemo/HelloNativeDemo.java 
package v2ch13.jnidemo;

class HelloNativeDemo {  
    void main() {
        int result = HelloNative.printf("Hello, Native World!\n");
        IO.println("Printed %d characters.".formatted(result));
    }

    static {  
        System.loadLibrary("HelloNative");
    }
}

Figure 13.1 gives a summary of the native code processing.

When you run this program, the message “Hello, Native World!” is displayed in a terminal window. This is the result from the C code. The next line, “Printed 21 characters.”, is produced by the Java code. We have taken the first step toward bridging the gap between the two languages!

If you run Linux, you must add the current directory to the library path. Either set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable: 

export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=v2ch13/jnidemo:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

or set the java.library.path system property:

java -Djava.library.path=v2ch13/jnidemo v2ch13.jnidemo.HelloNativeDemo

In summary, with JNI, you follow these steps to link a native method to a Java program:

  1. Declare a native method in a Java class.

  2. Run javac -h to get a header file with a C declaration for the method.

  3. Implement the native method in C.

  4. Place the code in a shared library.

  5. Load that library in your Java program.

java.lang.System1.0

  • void loadLibrary(String libname)

    loads the library with the given name. The library is located in the library search path. The exact method for locating the library depends on the operating system.

13.2. Using FFM to Call a Foreign Function

When using JNI, you have to write C code to access Java data structures, call the desired C functions, and to convert the result back to Java. Then you have to link the C code into platform-specific libraries. The API for accessing “foreign” functions and memory, developed under the code name “Project Panama,” greatly simplifies this process.

The program in Listing 13.5 is a very simple demonstration. It simply calls the printf function. No additional C code is necessary. The function is invoked through a MethodHandle object.

To access C functions, you first create a Linker object. The Linker can produce a Java method handle for a C function, given its address and type description.

The API has methods for translating Java objects into memory segments that you can pass to the C function. In the demo, you need to provide a char* with the characters from a Java String.

The memory is allocated in an Arena, so that its deallocation can be managed. Here, we use a confined arena. It is autocloseable, and the close method deallocates all allocated memory.

To compile and run the demo program, use these commands:

javac v2ch13/ffmdemo/HelloForeign.java
java --enable-preview --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED v2ch13.ffmdemo.HelloForeign

As you can see, this API is more Java-centric than JNI. All the conversion from Java to C is done in Java code, and you simply invoke the C library function from Java. In the following sections, you will see all the details about linkers, method handles, arenas, and memory segments.

Listing 13.5 v2ch13/ffmdemo/HelloForeign.java 
package v2ch13.ffmdemo;

import java.lang.invoke.*;
import java.lang.foreign.*;

public class HelloForeign {
    void main() throws Throwable {
        Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
        MethodHandle printf = linker.downcallHandle(
            linker.defaultLookup().findOrThrow("printf"),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, ValueLayout.ADDRESS));

        try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
            MemorySegment str = arena.allocateFrom("Hello, Foreign World!\n");
            int result = (int) printf.invoke(str);
            System.out.printf("Printed %d characters.%n", result);
        }
    }
}

13.3. Arenas

When interfacing with foreign functions, the Java part of the program needs to work with off-heap memory; that is, memory that was not allocated with a call to new.

An arena manages the lifetime of off-heap memory segments. You have seen one example in the preceding demo program. 

try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment str = arena.allocateFrom(. . .);
    . . .
} // Arena closed

The Arena class implements AutoCloseable, and the arena instance is closed when the try block ends. Any allocated segments become invalid afterwards. Attempting to access them causes an exception.

Here, a confined arena is used. The memory segments that a confined arena allocates can only be used in the arena’s owner thread, which is usually the thread in which the arena was created. The arena must also be closed in that thread. Otherwise an exception is thrown.

If memory segments must be shared by multiple threads, you cannot use a confined arena. One option is a shared arena, which is alive until you call close on it. It is up to you to close the arena at the appropriate time.

Alternatively, you can use an automatic arena. The garbage collector will eventually deallocate memory segments when they, and the arena, are no longer referenced. This is convenient, but less predictable. You cannot close an automatic arena.

MemorySegment segment = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(. . .);
. . .
segment = null; // Memory eventually deallocated

In this example, the automatic arena is only used once, to allocate a single segment.

Finally, the global arena is never closed, and the memory segments that it allocates are never deallocated.

You cannot deallocate individual memory segments. To deallocate a memory segment, you need to close the (confined or shared) arena that allocated it.

Table 13.1 summarizes the characteristics of the four arena types.

Table 13.1: Arena Types
Type Accessible from multiple threads How closed
Confined By calling close
Shared ✓ By calling close
Automatic ✓ By garbage collector
Global ✓ Never

java.lang.foreign.Arena22

  • static void ofConfined()

  • static void ofShared()

  • static void ofAuto()

    Yields a confined, shared, or automatic arena.

13.4. Memory Segments

A memory segment is a contiguous block of memory. It can be on the Java heap, managed by the garbage collector, or native, allocated off the Java heap. An off-heap memory segment has a fixed physical address. A heap segment, just like any Java object, has a reference through which it can be located, but no fixed address since the garbage collector may have moved it. For use with foreign functions, we are generally interested in off-heap memory segments.

You use an arena object to allocate an off-heap segment. As you already have seen, the call

String javaString = . . .;
MemorySegment cString = arena.allocateFrom(javaString);

encodes a Java string into UTF-8 and allocates a memory segment that holds the bytes, including a null terminator.

To allocate an array, you need to specify the element layout and the number of elements. You will see how to use the MemoryLayout interface in Section 13.5. For now, we will make use of the layout constants defined in the ValueLayout class. For example, here is how to allocate an array of float values:

MemorySegment audioIn = arena.allocate(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT, sampleCount);

If you already have the values in an array, use the allocateFrom method:

float[] samples = . . .;
MemorySegment audioOut = arena.allocateFrom(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT, samples);

When a memory segment is passed to a C function, the function receives the address of the segment. It can then process the contents of the string or array.

Conversely, suppose a C function has filled a memory segment with data. To turn a null-terminated UTF-8 string to a Java string, you pass an offset of 0 to the getString method:

String javaString = cString.getString(0);

To read or write at an array index, provide the memory layout and index:

float sample = audioIn.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT, i);
audioIn.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT, i, 0f);

You can also get a Java array with all values:

float[] samples = audioIn.toArray(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT);

The elements method yields a stream of memory segments, one for each element. You can map each of them into a value and then process the stream further.

DoubleStream samples = audioIn.elements(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT)
    .mapToDouble(m -> m.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT, 0));

The get method is like getAtIndex, but it takes a byte offset.

Note that the segment does not retain any information about the layout of the data inside. You need to provide the layout whenever you access or update the data.

java.lang.foreign.SegmentAllocator22

  • MemorySegment allocate(MemoryLayout layout)

    allocates off-heap memory with the given layout.

  • MemorySegment allocate(MemoryLayout elementLayout, long count)

    allocates an off-heap array with count elements of the given layout.

  • MemorySegment allocateFrom(ValueLayout.ofXxx elementLayout, xxx elements)

    Allocates off-heap memory holding the given primitive type elements.

  • MemorySegment allocateFrom(String str)

    allocates off-heap memory holding the null-terminated string with the UTF-8 encoding of str.

  • MemorySegment allocate(long byteSize, long byteAlignment)

    allocates an off-heap memory segment of the given size and alignment constraint.

  • Stream<MemorySegment> elements(MemoryLayout elementLayout)

    yields a sequential stream of slices with the given layout, taken from this memory segment.

java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment22

  • String getString(long offset)

    converts the null-terminated UTF-8 string at the given offset to a Java string.

  • xxx getAtIndex(ValueLayout.ofXxx layout, long index)

  • void setAtIndex(ValueLayout.ofXxx layout, long index, xxx value)

13.5. Memory Layout

In the preceding section, you have seen how to work with memory segments that hold UTF-8 strings and arrays of primitive type values.

In C, you use struct for more complex data. For example, the libsndfile library for processing sound files (https://github.com/libsndfile) yields a value of the following structure when opening a sound file:

struct SF_INFO {
    long frames;
    int samplerate;
    int channels;
    int format;
    int sections;
    int seekable;
} ;

You can define a layout for this structure as follows:

import static java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.*;
. . .
StructLayout SF_INFO = MemoryLayout.structLayout(
    JAVA_LONG.withName("frames"),
    JAVA_INT.withName("samplerate"),
    JAVA_INT.withName("channels"),
    JAVA_INT.withName("format"),
    JAVA_INT.withName("sections"),
    JAVA_INT.withName("seekable")
);

When matching up the C and Java types, the byte lengths need to match. But unsigned C types are mapped to their sized Java equivalents. If you process those values in Java, you need t to handle them as unsigned values yourself.

The expression Linker.nativeLinker().canonicalLayouts() yields a map from common type names to memory layouts. For example, on a 64-bit platform, "size_t" is mapped to a MemoryLayout with byte size 8, so you know to use a JAVA_LONG to represent the C type size_t in Java.

The following types are mapped: bool, char, short, int, long, long long, float, double, size_t, wchar_t, void*.

Suppose you have a memory segment info with the SF_INFO layout that was just declared. Here is how you can retrieve one of the components:

int channels = info.get(JAVA_INT,
    SF_INFO.byteOffset(PathElement.groupElement("channels")));

You have already seen the get method, which receives a memory layout and a byte offset. The StructLayout can determine the offset of each element. In this case, the offset is 12, since the "channels" element is preceded by elements of size 8 and 4.

In order to deal with nested structures, there are a number of interfaces to describe layouts—see Figure 13.2. The ValueLayout interface has subtypes ValueLayout.OfInt, ValueLayout.ofLong, and so on, one for each primitive type. The constants JAVA_INT, JAVA_LONG, and so on in the ValueLayout interface are instances of these types. The AddressLayout holds a memory address.

Figure 13.2: The MemoryLayout Hierarchy

As you have seen, a StructLayout describes the layout of C structures. Similarly, the UnionLayout describes C unions. This is not common, but if you need to deal with unions, you shouldn’t have any trouble using the UnionLayout interface. It is completely analogous to StructLayout.

The PaddingLayout describes padding bytes. You sometimes need to insert them to ensure that subsequent elements are properly aligned.

Let us use the SequenceLayout to model an array of structures:

long count = . . .;
SequenceLayout arrayOfPointLayout = MemoryLayout.sequenceLayout(count,
    MemoryLayout.structLayout(
        JAVA_FLOAT.withName("x"),
        JAVA_FLOAT.withName("y")));

To access an individual x- or y-component of the point with index i, we need to compute the byte offset:

long offset = arrayOfPointLayout.byteOffset(
    PathElement.sequenceElement(i), PathElement.groupElement("y"));

The byteOffset method receives a sequence of MemoryLayout.PathElement objects that navigate to the selected value.

Now, given a memory segment with that layout, we can get or set the value:

MemorySegment arrayOfPoints = Arena.global().allocate(arrayOfPointLayout);
arrayOfPoints.set(JAVA_FLOAT, offset, yvalue);

There is more to know about memory layouts and accessing values in memory segments, but what you have seen now suffices to pass complex data between Java and foreign functions. We will take that up in the following section. For more information, see Section 13.8.1.

13.6. Looking Up and Invoking Foreign Functions

When compiling C code, a linker carries out the essential step of combining the compiled files with precompiled code of library functions, producing an executable file.

The Linker abstraction in the FFM API doesn’t quite do the same thing. It looks up library functions and prepares MethodHandle objects to invoke them.

Actually, the “looking up” part is delegated to a SymbolLookup instance. To look up functions in a handful of standard libraries, use a default lookup:

Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker(); // The linker for the underlying platform
SymbolLookup stdlib = linker.defaultLookup();

The libraries that the default lookup knows about depend on the platform. On Linux, they include libc and libm. This lookup suffices for well-known functions such as printf and malloc.

For use with a specialized library, create a lookup as follows:

SymbolLookup sndfile = SymbolLookup.libraryLookup(
    "/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libsndfile.so", arena);

You specify the path to the library file (as a string or Path object), and an arena. The libraryLookup method loads the library. When the arena is closed, the library is unloaded.

There is also a loader lookup, returned by SymbolLookup.loaderLookup(), that looks up functions in libraries loaded through calls to System.load and System.loadLibrary.

Now you are ready to look up functions:

MemorySegment mallocAddr = stdlib.findOrThrow("malloc");
MemorySegment sfOpenAddr = sndfile.findOrThrow("sf_open");

The findOrThrow method throws a NoSuchElementException if the function was not found. There is also a find method that returns an Optional<MemorySegment> instead. The memory segment contains the address of the function to be invoked.

Many programmers look at the Java API as a model for good design, but in this particular instance, you might want to look twice.

The find method returns an Optional because surely that is the right thing to do when a lookup might fail. Or is it?

If you are in a similar situation when designing an API, consider whether you want to burden its users with Optional results. Of course, a lookup might fail. Java has a perfectly good mechanism for that—an exception.

An Optional is appropriate if there is a plausible action to take upon failure, such as substituting a default value, or skipping further processing. But if a library function isn't found, there is unlikely to be a local remedy, and an exception is the best outcome.

The findOrThrow method was added later to avoid the tedium of calling

MemorySegment mallocAddr = stdlib.find("malloc").orElseThrow();

It dispenses with the Optional, which is good. But what about the orThrow suffix? Fortunately, few exception-throwing methods have such a suffix in their name. The notable exception is Optional.orElseThrow, which was given a scary name so that programmers would consider alternatives, such as orElse or map.

When you find yourself implementing a method whose failure is unlikely to be curable locally, don’t return an Optional (and of course, don’t return null). Just throw an exception. Without uglifying the method name.

Having found the memory address of the function to be invoked, we are ready to create a method handle for the invocation. A method handle is an object through which you can provide arguments, invoke a method, and obtain the returned value. It is similar to a Method object in the java.lang.reflect package, but it can also invoke native methods.

To get the method handle, provide the parameter and return types:

// void* malloc(size_t)
MethodHandle mallocHandle = linker.downcallHandle(mallocAddr,
    FunctionDescriptor.of(ADDRESS, JAVA_LONG));

// SNDFILE* sf_open(const char *path, int mode, SF_INFO *sfinfo)
MethodHandle sfOpenHandle = linker.downcallHandle(sfOpenAddr,
    FunctionDescriptor.of(ADDRESS, ADDRESS, JAVA_INT, ADDRESS));

For a function with return type void, you use FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid instead:

// void free(void *ptr)
MethodHandle freeHandle = linker.downcallHandle(
    stdlib.findOrThrow("free"),
    FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(ADDRESS));

Here, we ask for a downcall handle for calling a C function from Java code. In Section 13.7, you will see how to use memory handles for calling a Java method from C.

When passing a pointer to a C function, or receiving a pointer result, you use ValueLayout.ADDRESS. The type of the memory block is immaterial.

You must describe the function return type and parameter types accurately. The linker cannot verify this information. If you provide incorrect information, the virtual machine may crash.

Finally, we are ready to invoke the method.

MemorySegment block = mallocHandle.invoke(blockSize);

MemorySegment info = arena.allocate(SF_INFO);
MemorySegment cInputPath = arena.allocateFrom(inputFile);
MemorySegment inFile = (MemorySegment) sf_open.invoke(cInputPath, SFM_READ, info);

When a foreign function returns a pointer, it is wrapped into a zero-length memory segment. To read from the segment, you need some external knowledge of its size and structure.

For example, you know the size of the memory block allocated by malloc, so you can set

block = block.reinterpret(blockSize);

Clearly, this is a potentially unsafe operation. If you use any memory segment outside its actual bounds, you can corrupt unrelated memory or crash the virtual machine.

The jextract tool, which you can find at https://github.com/openjdk/jextract, automatically generates memory layouts and wrappers for foreign calls from C header files.

You now know enough about the FFM API to write nontrivial programs that call a native library. The program in Listing 13.6 is a typical example. It uses the libsndfile library to read a sound file, reverses the samples, and writes the result to another file.

The program first sets up the layout for the SF_INFO structure and memory handles for four C functions:

SNDFILE* sf_open(const char *path, int mode, SF_INFO *sfinfo)
int sf_close(SNDFILE *sndfile)
sf_count_t sf_read_float(SNDFILE *sndfile, float *ptr, sf_count_t items)
sf_count_t sf_write_float(SNDFILE *sndfile, const float *ptr, sf_count_t items)

Then the program opens the input file and retrieves the number of frames and channels from the SF_INFO structure.

Next, the call to sf_read_float fills a pre-allocated memory segment with the sample data.

For ease of processing in Java, the memory segment is converted to a Java array. After processing, the data is written to the output file.

Listing 13.6 v2ch13/sound/SoundFileReverser.java 
package v2ch13.sound;

import module java.base;

import static java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.*;

class SoundFileReverser {
    static final int SFM_READ = 0x10;
    static final int SFM_WRITE = 0x20;

    void main(String[] args) throws Throwable {
        String inputFile = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "sound/input.mp3";
        String outputFile = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "sound/output.mp3";

        Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
        SymbolLookup sndfile = SymbolLookup.libraryLookup(
            "/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libsndfile.so", Arena.ofAuto());

        StructLayout SF_INFO = MemoryLayout.structLayout(
            JAVA_LONG.withName("frames"),
            JAVA_INT.withName("samplerate"),
            JAVA_INT.withName("channels"),
            JAVA_INT.withName("format"),
            JAVA_INT.withName("sections"),
            JAVA_INT.withName("seekable")
        );

        MethodHandle sf_open = linker.downcallHandle(
            sndfile.findOrThrow("sf_open"),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(ADDRESS, ADDRESS, JAVA_INT, ADDRESS)
        );

        MethodHandle sf_close = linker.downcallHandle(
            sndfile.findOrThrow("sf_close"),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_INT, ADDRESS)
        );

        MethodHandle sf_readf_float = linker.downcallHandle(
            sndfile.findOrThrow("sf_readf_float"),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS, ADDRESS, JAVA_LONG)
        );

        MethodHandle sf_writef_float = linker.downcallHandle(
            sndfile.findOrThrow("sf_writef_float"),
            FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS, ADDRESS, JAVA_LONG)
        );

        try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
            MemorySegment info = arena.allocate(SF_INFO);
            MemorySegment cInputPath = arena.allocateFrom(inputFile);

            // Open sound file
            MemorySegment inFile = (MemorySegment) sf_open.invoke(cInputPath, SFM_READ, info);
            if (inFile == MemorySegment.NULL)
                throw new RuntimeException("sf_open: Failed for " + inputFile);
            long frames = info.get(JAVA_LONG,
                SF_INFO.byteOffset(PathElement.groupElement("frames")));
            int channels = info.get(JAVA_INT,
                SF_INFO.byteOffset(PathElement.groupElement("channels")));
            long totalSamples = frames * channels;

            // Allocate native memory for audio samples
            MemorySegment audioIn = arena.allocate(JAVA_FLOAT, totalSamples);

            // Read samples
            long actualFrames = (long) sf_readf_float.invoke(
                inFile, audioIn, frames);
            if (frames != actualFrames)
                throw new RuntimeException(
                    "sf_readf_float: Expected %d frames but read %d frames."
                    .formatted(frames, actualFrames));

            // Copy native array to Java and process
            float[] audioSamples = audioIn.toArray(JAVA_FLOAT);
            
            // Reverse the frames
            for (int f = 0; f < frames / 2; f++) {
                for (int c = 0; c < channels; c++) {
                    int i = f * channels + c;
                    int j = (int)((frames - 1 - f) * channels + c);
                    float temp = audioSamples[i];
                    audioSamples[i] = audioSamples[j];
                    audioSamples[j] = temp;
                }
            }

            // Write to sound file
            MemorySegment cOutputPath = arena.allocateFrom(outputFile);
            MemorySegment outFile = (MemorySegment) sf_open.invoke(
                cOutputPath, SFM_WRITE, info);
            if (outFile == MemorySegment.NULL)
                throw new RuntimeException("sf_open: Failed for " + outputFile);

            // Copy Java array to native and write
            MemorySegment audioOut = arena.allocateFrom(JAVA_FLOAT, audioSamples);

            actualFrames = (long) sf_writef_float.invoke(outFile, audioOut, frames);
            if (frames != actualFrames)
                throw new RuntimeException(
                    "sf_writef_float: Expected to write %d frames but wrote %d frames."
                    .formatted(frames, actualFrames));

            sf_close.invoke(inFile);
            int error = (int) sf_close.invoke(outFile);
            if (error != 0)
                throw new RuntimeException("sf_close: Failed with error code " + error);
            IO.println("Reversed " + inputFile + " to  " + outputFile);
        }
    }
}

13.7. Callbacks

Sometimes, you call a foreign function that wants to call another function when an event occurs; for example, when input is detected at a microphone or camera. I would prefer to demonstrate this with a realistic example, but there is a fair amount of boilerplate and configuration required. Instead, here is an example with the qsort function from the standard library:

void qsort(void *base, size_t nmemb, size_t size,
    int (*compar)(const void *, const void *));

The last parameter is a pointer to a function that is being called whenever two elements are compared.

We want the following Java method to be called back:

static int comp(MemorySegment a, MemorySegment b) {
    return Float.compare(a.get(JAVA_FLOAT, 0), b.get(JAVA_FLOAT, 0));
}

As already mentioned, keep in mind that this is a toy example to show the mechanics of a callback. One would not normally split up this work between Java and C.

The following code snippet gets a method handle to the foreign function in the usual way:

Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
MethodHandle qsort = linker.downcallHandle(
    linker.defaultLookup().findOrThrow("qsort"),
    FunctionDescriptor.of(ADDRESS, JAVA_LONG, JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS));

When invoking the function, we supply an array, its length, the size of each element in bytes, and the address of the callback.

To produce that address, first get a MemoryHandle to the static Java method:

MethodHandle compHandle = MethodHandles.lookup()
    .findStatic(UpcallDemo.class, "comp",
        MethodType.methodType(
            int.class, MemorySegment.class, MemorySegment.class));

This has nothing to do with foreign functions. One can get a method handle to any Java method, and invoke it later.

The linker can generate stub code for a C function that then invokes the method handle of the callback:

MemorySegment compStub = linker.upcallStub(
    compHandle,
    FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_INT,
        ADDRESS.withTargetLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT),
        ADDRESS.withTargetLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT)),
    arena);

Note the withTargetLayout calls. They configure the memory layout so that the linker can generate code for configuring the MemorySegment instances that the Java callback receives. If you don’t do that, the calls to a.get(JAVA_FLOAT, 0) and b.get(JAVA_FLOAT, 0) in the Java callback will fail because the memory segments a and b will have size zero.

Finally, you are ready to call the foreign function with the callback address:

float[] samples = . . .;
MemorySegment csamples = arena.allocateFrom(JAVA_FLOAT, samples);
qsort.invoke(csamples, samples.length, JAVA_FLOAT.byteSize(), compStub);

You will find the complete program in Listing 13.7

Listing 13.7 v2ch13/upcall/UpcallDemo.java 
package v2ch13.upcall;

import module java.base;

import static java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.*;

class UpcallDemo {
    static int comp(MemorySegment a, MemorySegment b) {
        return Float.compare(a.get(JAVA_FLOAT, 0), b.get(JAVA_FLOAT, 0));
    }
    
    void main() throws Throwable {
        Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
        MethodHandle qsort = linker.downcallHandle(
            linker.defaultLookup().findOrThrow("qsort"),
            FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(ADDRESS, JAVA_LONG, JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS));

        MethodHandle compHandle = MethodHandles.lookup()
            .findStatic(UpcallDemo.class, "comp", 
                MethodType.methodType(
                    int.class, MemorySegment.class, MemorySegment.class));

        MemorySegment compStub = linker.upcallStub(
            compHandle,
            FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_INT,
                ADDRESS.withTargetLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT),
                ADDRESS.withTargetLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_FLOAT)),
            Arena.ofAuto());

        float[] samples = new float[100];
        RandomGenerator generator = RandomGenerator.getDefault();
        for (int i = 0; i < samples.length; i++)
            samples[i] = generator.nextFloat();
        try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
            MemorySegment csamples = arena.allocateFrom(JAVA_FLOAT, samples);
            qsort.invoke(csamples,
                samples.length, JAVA_FLOAT.byteSize(), compStub);
            samples = csamples.toArray(JAVA_FLOAT);
            IO.println(Arrays.toString(samples));
        }
    }    
}

13.8. Advanced Topics

You have now seen enough about the FFM API to write nontrivial programs. The API provides solutions for a number of more complex situations that we will examine in the following sections.

13.8.1. Accessing Memory With Variable Handles

A variable handle allows getting or setting a single value, or multiple values that are specified by coordinates. These could be array indices or map keys, or any other objects that describe the location of a value.

VarHandle vh = . . .;
Object value = vh.get(coord1, coord2, . . .);
vh.set(coord1, coord2, . . ., newValue);

In Section 13.5, you have seen how to access elements in a struct by computing the element offset from a layout. We looked at the example of the layout of the SF_INFO structure that has a channels element.

long channelsOffset = SF_INFO.byteOffset(PathElement.groupElement("channels"));
int channels = info.get(JAVA_INT, channelsOffset);

Instead of computing offsets, you can use variable handles. For example, here is a variable handle to the channels element:

VarHandle channelsHandle = SF_INFO.varHandle(PathElement.groupElement("channels"));

This variable handle has a single “coordinate”—the memory segment holding the structure. Here is how you look inside a memory segment info to read the field value:

int channels = (int) channelsHandle.get(info);

Using a variable handle isn't any simpler than computing a byte offset, but it is a bit safer. After all, it is easy enough to accidentally use the wrong offset.

Now consider an array layout:

long count = . . .;
StructLayout pointLayout = MemoryLayout.structLayout(
    JAVA_FLOAT.withName("x"),
    JAVA_FLOAT.withName("y"));
SequenceLayout arrayOfPointLayout = MemoryLayout.sequenceLayout(count, pointLayout);

Here is a variable handle for the x-coordinate of a point in the array:

VarHandle xHandle = arrayOfPointLayout.varHandle(
    PathElement.sequenceElement(),
    PathElement.groupElement("x"));

The PathElement.sequenceElement() call returns an open path element which gives rise to another coordinate in the variable handle. Now you can access the ith x-coordinate as:

MemorySegment pointSegment = . . .;
long i = . . .;
float xi = (float) xHandle.get(pointSegment, i);

Now suppose you have an array of pointers, each to a point structure.

MemoryLayout arrayOfPointPointersLayout = MemoryLayout.sequenceLayout(count,
    ValueLayout.ADDRESS.withTargetLayout(pointLayout));

Note the withTargetLayout method that attaches the layout of the memory segment to which the address points. We did not do that in the past with ADDRESS because we could not make use of the type information. But there is a special path element for following a pointer:

VarHandle xHandle = arrayOfPointPointersLayout.varHandle(
    PathElement.sequenceElement(),
    PathElement.dereferenceElement(),
    PathElement.groupElement("x"));

A MemoryLayout can also produce a method handle for computing byte offsets, which is potentially convenient for paths with open path elements.

MethodHandle xByteOffsetHandle = arrayOfPointLayout.byteOffsetHandle(
    PathElement.sequenceElement(),
    PathElement.groupElement("x"));

Now you can compute an offset like this:

long offset = (long) xByteOffsetHandle(0, i);

The first argument is the base offset, usually zero.

Of course, this doesn't work when the path doesn't have indirections.

13.8.2. Calling a Foreign Varargs Function

In C, functions with variable arguments use a special calling convention. The classic example is

int printf(const char *format, ...);

In order to call such a function, the FunctionDescriptor must know where the fixed arguments end and the variable arguments start.

You must make a separate method handle for each pattern of arguments. For example, suppose you’d like to call

printf("Hello, %s! Next year, you'll be %d\n", name, age);

You will be passing the format string, another string, and an integer.

MethodHandle printf = linker.downcallHandle(
    linker.defaultLookup().findOrThrow("printf"),
        FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_INT, ADDRESS, ADDRESS, JAVA_INT),
        Linker.Option.firstVariadicArg(1));

The linker option specfies the index of the first variable parameter.

13.8.3. Capturing errno

Some C functions signal an error condition by placing an integer error code in a location that can be retrieved with the errno macro.

To capture this value, use another linker option:

MethodHandle fopen = linker.downcallHandle(
    linker.defaultLookup().findOrThrow("fopen"),
    FunctionDescriptor.of(ADDRESS, ADDRESS, ADDRESS),
    Linker.Option.captureCallState("errno"));

Before calling the foreign function, allocate a memory segment for the capture state:

StructLayout captureStateLayout = Linker.Option.captureStateLayout();
MemorySegment captureState = arena.allocate(captureStateLayout);

Pass that memory segment as the first argument when invoking the method handle:

var result = (MemorySegment) fopen.invoke(captureState,
    arena.allocateFrom("woozle.txt"),
    arena.allocateFrom("rw"));

Upon return, you can read errno from the capture state:

long errnoOffset = capturedStateLayout.byteOffset(PathElement.groupElement("errno"));
int errno = (int) capturedState.get(JAVA_INT, errnoOffset);

Or, with a variable handle:

VarHandle errnoHandle = captureStateLayout.varHandle(PathElement.groupElement("errno"));
int errno = (int) errnoHandle.get(capturedState, 0);

To get the values that can be captured, look at

List<MemoryLayout> layouts = Linker.Option.captureStateLayout().memberLayouts();

On Linux, you currently only get errno.

You have now reached the end of the second volume of Core Java, completing a long journey in which you encountered many advanced APIs. I started out with topics that every Java programmer needs to know: streams, XML, networking, databases, and internationalization. I concluded with very technical chapters on security, annotation processing, advanced graphics, and native methods. I hope that you enjoyed your tour through the vast breadth of the Java APIs, and that you will be able to apply your newly gained knowledge in your projects.
